alt: A 2 by 4 grid and the flat list holding the same nine values row after row. A query picks a cell, and the index r * 4 + c locates it in the list. Its right neighbor is the next index, its lower neighbor is four indexes further on. In the edge presets a neighbor does not exist: stepping one index past the last column would land on the first cell of the next row, so the column check comes first.

steps.caption: The grid has 2 rows and 4 columns. `cells` holds the same 8 values, row after row, so cell (r, c) sits at index `r * 4 + c`.
Cell (0, 1) is at index 0 * 4 + 1 = 1, and `cells[1]` is 2.
Column 1 + 1 is 2, less than 4, so a right neighbor exists. It is the next index, 1 + 1 = 2: `cells[2]` is 3.
Row 0 + 1 is 1, less than 2. A row is 4 cells long, so the cell below is 4 indexes on: 1 + 4 = 5, and `cells[5]` is 6.
The grid has 2 rows and 4 columns. `cells` holds the same 8 values, row after row, so cell (r, c) sits at index `r * 4 + c`.
Cell (0, 3) is at index 0 * 4 + 3 = 3, and `cells[3]` is 4.
Index 3 + 1 is 4, which is cell (1, 0) on the next row, so the check `c + 1 < cols` fails first: column 3 + 1 is 4, not less than 4. No right neighbor.
Row 0 + 1 is 1, less than 2. A row is 4 cells long, so the cell below is 4 indexes on: 3 + 4 = 7, and `cells[7]` is 8.
The program prints `cell 4 right none down 8`.
The grid has 2 rows and 4 columns. `cells` holds the same 8 values, row after row, so cell (r, c) sits at index `r * 4 + c`.
Cell (1, 3) is at index 1 * 4 + 3 = 7, and `cells[7]` is 8.
Column 3 + 1 is 4, not less than 4, so there is no right neighbor. Index 7 + 1 is 8, past the end of the list.
Row 1 + 1 is 2, not less than 2, so there is no cell below. Index 7 + 4 would be 11, past the end of the list.
The program prints `cell 8 right none down none`.
